column2: wanting to cut an apple with a big kitchen knife
column3: ask a grown-up first; cut on a chopping board, fingers curled away from the blade, cutting away from your body
column4: a slip of a sharp knife can cut deeply, and a board stops the knife and the apple from sliding

column2: a knife has fallen off the counter
column3: step back and let it fall; never try to catch a falling knife
column4: grabbing at a falling blade is how hands get cut badly

column2: a sharp knife is lying in the soapy washing-up water
column3: never leave or reach for knives hidden under bubbles; wash them separately and put them away at once
column4: someone putting a hand into the water cannot see the blade and gets cut

column2: carrying a knife across the kitchen
column3: hold it pointing down, by your side, and walk; say "knife" if someone is close behind
column4: if you trip or bump someone, a pointed-down knife is less likely to stab anyone

column2: passing a knife to someone
column3: lay it on the counter for them to pick up, or hand it handle first
column4: holding out the blade puts the other person's hand on the sharp edge

column2: a blunt knife that keeps slipping on a tomato
column3: tell a grown-up; a blunt knife is not safer, it slips and needs more force
column4: you push harder with a blunt knife, so when it slips it cuts you

column2: using a grater for cheese
column3: stop before the piece gets small, and keep fingertips and knuckles away from the holes
column4: graters take skin off fingers very easily

column2: a blender is blocked and you want to poke it
column3: switch it off and unplug it before touching anything inside, and never put hands or a spoon in while it runs
column4: the blades are very sharp and can start again if it is still plugged in

column2: opening a tin with a tin opener
column3: let a grown-up help; do not lick the lid or run fingers along the edge
column4: the cut edge of a tin lid is as sharp as a razor

column2: peeling potatoes with a peeler
column3: peel away from yourself, holding the potato firmly on a board
column4: peelers slip and nick the hand holding the food

column2: a can or jar lid you cannot open
column3: ask for help instead of using a knife to lever it
column4: a knife used as a lever snaps or slips into your hand

column2: wanting a snack from a high cupboard
column3: use a steady step stool, not a chair on wheels or the counter edge, or ask someone tall
column4: climbing on unstable things is a common cause of falls at home

column2: helping at the hob with a pot of boiling pasta
column3: turn pan handles inwards, away from the edge, and stand well back when the lid comes off
column4: a handle sticking out gets knocked and boiling water burns badly; steam scalds too

column2: frying something and the oil starts to smoke
column3: turn off the heat and call a grown-up; never put water on hot oil
column4: water on hot oil explodes into a fireball of burning fat

column2: a pan of oil catches fire
column3: turn off the heat if you can, cover it with a lid or damp tea towel, leave the room, shut the door and call for help
column4: fire needs air; water spreads oil fires and makes them worse

column2: taking a tray out of the oven
column3: use dry oven gloves on both hands; never a damp cloth
column4: wet cloth carries heat straight to your skin and burns you

column2: a pan has just come off the hob
column3: treat it as hot even if it looks cold, and leave it where it is
column4: metal stays hot long after the heat is off

column2: wearing long loose sleeves while stirring a pot
column3: roll up sleeves and tie back long hair before cooking
column4: loose cloth and hair can catch fire on a gas flame or drag a pan

column2: wanting to taste food straight from the spoon in the pot
column3: blow on it and let it cool first, and use a clean spoon so you do not put your mouth's germs back
column4: hot food burns the mouth, and germs spread to everyone's dinner

column2: raw chicken juice on the chopping board
column3: wash the board, knife and hands with hot soapy water before using them for anything else
column4: raw meat carries germs like salmonella that cause food poisoning

column2: tasting raw cookie dough or cake batter
column3: wait until it is baked
column4: raw egg and raw flour can carry germs that make you ill

column2: a grown-up says the kitchen is not a place to run
column3: walk in the kitchen and play somewhere else while cooking happens
column4: knives, hot pans and slippery floors make running there dangerous

column2: something spilt on the kitchen floor
column3: wipe it up straight away or tell someone
column4: a wet or greasy floor makes people slip, sometimes carrying hot things

column2: milk smells sour
column3: do not drink it; tell a grown-up and check the date on the carton
column4: spoiled food can make you sick

column2: bread has small green or white fuzzy spots
column3: throw the whole loaf away, not just the spot
column4: mould spreads threads through soft food further than you can see

column2: leftover pizza left out on the table all night
column3: ask a grown-up; cooked food left warm for hours can be unsafe
column4: germs grow fast at room temperature

column2: the fridge door left open
column3: close it properly
column4: food warms up and spoils, and it wastes electricity

column2: washing hands before helping to cook
column3: wash with soap for about 20 seconds, the time of singing "Happy Birthday" twice
column4: hands carry germs onto food

column2: a little brother wants to try your peanut butter but has an allergy
column3: never share food with someone who has an allergy, and tell a grown-up if they eat it
column4: allergies can cause dangerous reactions, even from a tiny amount

column2: warming food in the microwave in a metal bowl or with foil
column3: use only microwave-safe dishes; no metal, foil or dishes with gold rims
column4: metal makes sparks and can start a fire

column2: heating an egg in its shell in the microwave
column3: never microwave a whole egg in its shell
column4: steam builds up inside and the egg explodes, sometimes in your face

column2: taking a bowl of soup out of the microwave
column3: use oven gloves, stir it and wait a moment; peel cling film away from you
column4: the bowl and steam can be very hot, and microwaves heat unevenly with hot spots

column2: the microwave is running with nothing inside
column3: never run it empty; stop it if you notice
column4: with nothing to absorb the energy, the microwave can be damaged

column2: something catches fire inside the microwave
column3: keep the door shut, switch it off at the wall and call a grown-up
column4: the fire runs out of air if the door stays closed

column2: heating a sealed jar or a closed container
column3: take the lid off or leave a gap
column4: pressure builds and the lid or jar can burst

column2: the oven door is open and a little sister is near
column3: keep small children away and close the door quickly
column4: the door and inside are hot enough to burn skin instantly

column2: a smell of gas in the kitchen
column3: do not switch lights or anything on or off, do not light anything; open windows, leave the house and tell a grown-up or call the gas emergency number from outside
column4: a spark can ignite gas and cause an explosion

column2: a gas hob flame has gone out but the gas is still on
column3: turn the knob off and tell a grown-up; do not relight it yourself
column4: unburnt gas fills the room and can explode

column2: an induction or ceramic hob looks dark and cool
column3: do not touch; a hob can stay hot after it is switched off
column4: a black glass top does not show the heat

column2: filling the kettle to make tea
column3: unplug it before filling, fill only to the line, and keep the cord tucked away from the edge
column4: a dangling cord can pull a full boiling kettle onto someone

column2: pouring from a kettle that just boiled
column3: pour slowly away from your body, holding the cup on the counter, not in your hand
column4: boiling water causes serious scalds

column2: a toddler is near the kitchen counter while tea is being made
column3: keep hot drinks out of reach and never carry a hot drink while holding a little one
column4: a hot cup of tea can scald a small child even twenty minutes later

column2: toast is stuck in the toaster
column3: switch off and unplug it, wait for it to cool, then lift it with wooden tongs; never a metal knife or fork
column4: a metal knife inside a toaster can give a deadly electric shock

column2: toast starts smoking in the toaster
column3: press the cancel lever and unplug it; do not leave it
column4: burning toast can catch fire and set off smoke alarms

column2: crumbs pile up in the toaster
column3: ask a grown-up to empty the crumb tray when it is unplugged and cold
column4: old crumbs can catch fire

column2: loading knives into the dishwasher
column3: put knives and forks with points down in the basket, or knives flat in the top
column4: you or someone unloading could be stabbed by an upward point

column2: opening the dishwasher just after it finished
column3: wait a few minutes and open it slowly, standing back
column4: a cloud of hot steam can scald your face

column2: dishwasher tablets look like sweets
column3: keep them in a high cupboard and never let little ones play with them
column4: they are strong chemicals that burn the mouth and throat

column2: the dishwasher door is down and you walk past
column3: close it
column4: people trip over an open dishwasher door and fall onto the knives

column2: a little brother wants to hide inside the washing machine or tumble dryer
column3: never let anyone climb into a washer, dryer or old fridge; keep the doors shut
column4: children can get trapped and suffocate, and the door may not open from inside

column2: laundry pods look squishy and colourful
column3: keep them locked away from little children; they are never toys
column4: they burst in the mouth and the soap is poisonous

column2: helping to sort laundry
column3: check pockets for tissues, pens and coins, and separate whites from colours
column4: tissues shred everywhere, pens stain, and a red sock can turn white clothes pink

column2: the washing machine is shaking and walking across the floor
column3: stop it and tell a grown-up
column4: the load may be unbalanced and it can damage the machine or pull the hose

column2: cleaning fluff from the tumble dryer filter
column3: clean the lint filter after each use, with a grown-up's say-so
column4: fluff builds up and can start a fire

column2: water on the floor around the washing machine
column3: keep away from plugs and switches and tell a grown-up
column4: water and electricity together can give a shock

column2: licking an ice lolly straight from the freezer or touching frozen metal with your tongue
column3: let it warm a little; never put your tongue on frozen metal
column4: wet skin freezes and sticks, tearing when you pull away

column2: a soda can put in the freezer to cool quickly
column3: take it out within a short time or do not put it there
column4: liquid expands when it freezes and the can can burst

column2: a plug socket in the wall
column3: never push anything but a proper plug into it: no fingers, pins, keys or pencils
column4: mains electricity can kill

column2: pulling a plug out by its cord
column3: switch off and pull by the plug itself, not the cable
column4: tugging the cable damages wires inside and can cause shocks or fire

column2: wet hands and a hair dryer
column3: dry your hands before touching plugs or switches
column4: water conducts electricity into your body

column2: using a hair dryer or phone charger in the bathroom near the bath
column3: never use mains electrical things near a full bath or sink; in the UK and Ireland bathrooms have pull-cord switches for that reason
column4: a device falling into water can electrocute the person in it

column2: a cable is frayed with wires showing
column3: do not touch or use it; tell a grown-up
column4: bare wires can shock you or spark a fire

column2: a plug or socket is hot or smells of burning
column3: switch off at the wall if safe and tell a grown-up at once
column4: it is a sign of an electrical fault that can start a fire

column2: plugging many adaptors into one socket
column3: do not stack adaptors; use one extension lead and ask a grown-up
column4: too much current overheats the socket

column2: a charger left under the pillow at night
column3: charge phones and tablets on a hard surface, not under bedding
column4: chargers get hot and bedding can catch fire

column2: a power cut happens in the evening
column3: stay calm, use a torch rather than candles, and keep the fridge closed
column4: torches are safe in the dark; candles start fires; a closed fridge keeps food cold for hours

column2: plugs look different on holiday
column3: the UK and Ireland have three square pins, the USA and Canada two flat pins, Australia and New Zealand slanted pins; use a proper travel adaptor
column4: forcing a wrong plug can damage it and cause shocks

column2: kites or climbing near overhead power lines
column3: never fly a kite or climb a tree near power lines; if a kite gets caught, let it go
column4: electricity can jump to you along the string or branch

column2: a fallen power line in the street after a storm
column3: stay at least as far away as a bus is long and tell a grown-up to call the emergency number
column4: a fallen line can still be live and kill even through the ground

column2: running a bath
column3: turn on cold first, then add hot, and test the water with your elbow before getting in
column4: water from the hot tap can scald; elbows feel heat better than hands

column2: a baby or toddler in the bath
column3: never leave a young child alone in the bath, not even for a moment to answer the phone
column4: a small child can drown in a few centimetres of water in seconds

column2: getting out of the bath or shower
column3: step onto a mat and hold the side
column4: wet tiles and baths are very slippery

column2: a tap left running in the bathroom
column3: turn it off when you are done; turn off the tap while brushing teeth
column4: it wastes water and the sink can overflow and flood the floor

column2: the bath or sink is overflowing
column3: turn off the tap and pull the plug, keep away from electrical things and tell a grown-up
column4: water can leak through the ceiling and touch electrical wiring

column2: a dripping tap
column3: tell a grown-up so it can be fixed
column4: a drip wastes a lot of water over days

column2: a bucket of water left on the floor
column3: empty buckets after use
column4: toddlers can fall headfirst into a bucket and drown

column2: the toilet is blocked
column3: stop flushing and tell a grown-up
column4: flushing again makes it overflow

column2: putting things down the toilet
column3: only toilet paper goes down the toilet: not wipes, toys or cotton buds
column4: other things block the pipes

column2: a pipe bursts and water pours through the ceiling
column3: tell a grown-up at once; they know where the stopcock or main water valve is
column4: turning off the water stops the flood

column2: slamming a door when angry
column3: close doors gently
column4: slamming can trap fingers and break glass, and it scares people

column2: a little sister has her fingers near the hinge side of a door
column3: check behind and around a door before closing it
column4: the hinge side crushes fingers badly

column2: a swinging door with someone behind it
column3: open doors slowly and look through glass if there is any
column4: you can hit someone on the other side

column2: locking yourself in the bathroom
column3: do not lock the door if you are little or unsure the lock opens easily; tell someone if you get stuck
column4: grown-ups may need to get in if you feel ill or get trapped

column2: a fire door in a block of flats is propped open
column3: leave fire doors closed
column4: they stop smoke and fire spreading along the corridor

column2: a glass door or patio door that looks open
column3: slow down near glass doors; look for stickers on them
column4: people walk into clean glass and it can break and cut

column2: wanting to lean out of an upstairs window
column3: never lean out or sit on a windowsill; keep furniture away from windows
column4: falls from windows badly hurt or kill children every year

column2: a fly screen in the window
column3: do not lean on it
column4: a fly screen keeps insects out but will not hold a person

column2: blind cords hanging near a bed
column3: tie them up high or ask a grown-up to fit a cleat
column4: young children can get the cord around their neck and strangle

column2: opening a window in winter while the heating is on
column3: open it for a short while to air the room, then close it
column4: a short airing changes air without wasting much heat

column2: a window lock and key
column3: know where the key is kept so the window can be opened in a fire
column4: windows are a second way out if the door is blocked

column2: playing ball on a balcony
column3: do not climb, sit on or lean over the railing; do not put chairs or boxes against it
column4: a child can climb up and fall

column2: throwing things off a balcony
column3: never throw or drop anything from a balcony
column4: even a small object falling from a height can seriously hurt someone below

column2: a balcony door closing behind you
column3: keep it from locking you out, and call to someone inside if you get stuck
column4: you can be shut outside in the cold

column2: toys left on the stairs
column3: keep stairs clear; carry toys up, not leave them on steps
column4: people trip on stairs and fall all the way down

column2: running down the stairs in socks
column3: walk, hold the handrail and wear slippers with grip
column4: socks slip on wood and carpet

column2: carrying a big laundry basket down stairs
column3: carry loads you can see over and keep one hand on the rail
column4: you cannot see the steps behind a big load

column2: a stair gate for a baby brother
column3: close the gate behind you every time; do not climb over it
column4: toddlers fall down stairs when the gate is left open

column2: sliding down the banister
column3: use the stairs normally
column4: you can fall off sideways from a height

column2: climbing up the bookshelf or chest of drawers
column3: never climb furniture; ask a grown-up to fix tall furniture to the wall
column4: it can tip over and crush a child

column2: a big TV on a stand
column3: do not climb on or pull the TV stand; TVs should be fixed or strapped
column4: falling TVs injure and kill small children

column2: leaning back on two chair legs
column3: sit with all four legs on the floor
column4: the chair slips and you hit your head

column2: jumping on the bed or sofa
column3: jump only where it is allowed, never near windows or sharp corners
column4: you can fall off and hit your head, and springs break

column2: bunk beds
column3: only one person on the top bunk, use the ladder, no play on top; little ones under six not on the top
column4: falls from bunk beds are a common injury

column2: sharp corner of a glass coffee table at toddler head height
column3: watch toddlers near it; grown-ups can fit corner guards
column4: toddlers fall against corners and cut their heads

column2: pulling a heavy drawer all the way out
column3: pull drawers gently and only partly
column4: it can fall on your feet, and opening many drawers can tip the chest

column2: a recliner or folding chair
column3: keep fingers clear of the folding parts
column4: the mechanism pinches and crushes fingers

column2: your room is a mess and you cannot find your homework
column3: have a place for each thing and tidy a little every day
column4: it is quicker to find things and you do not trip

column2: making your bed in the morning
column3: pull the duvet straight and plump the pillow
column4: a tidy room feels calmer and it helps the family

column2: it is your turn to set the table
column3: fork on the left, knife on the right with its blade facing the plate, spoon on the right of the knife, glass above the knife
column4: this is the usual way in English-speaking homes, and everyone can find what they need

column2: clearing the table after dinner
column3: carry a few plates at a time, scrape leftovers into the bin or food caddy, stack them by the sink
column4: carrying too much leads to dropping and breaking

column2: washing up by hand
column3: use warm, not scalding, soapy water, wash glasses first and greasy pans last, rinse and dry
column4: cleaner things first keeps the water clean longer

column2: drying dishes with a tea towel
column3: use a clean dry towel and put things away where they belong
column4: wet dishes stacked away can go mouldy

column2: vacuuming the floor
column3: pick up small things, cords and socks first; never vacuum near someone's hair or pets' tails
column4: the vacuum sucks up small things and can break, and it tangles hair

column2: taking out the rubbish
column3: tie the bag, carry it with hands away from your legs, and put recycling in the right bin
column4: broken glass or sharp tins in the bag can cut your legs; sorting recycling saves resources

column2: recycling
column3: rinse tins and bottles, flatten boxes, and check what your council or town accepts
column4: dirty or wrong items can spoil a whole load of recycling

column2: feeding the family pet as a chore
column3: give the right amount at the same time each day and fresh water
column4: pets need regular care and depend on you

column2: watering houseplants
column3: water when the soil is dry to touch; do not drown them
column4: too much water rots roots

column2: your parent asks you to help but you are in the middle of a game
column3: pause the game, help, then go back
column4: everyone in a family shares the work

column2: you are paid pocket money for chores
column3: do the job properly, not quickly and badly
column4: money is earned by doing a job well

column2: folding laundry
column3: fold clothes and put them in your drawers; match socks
column4: clothes stay neat and do not crease

column2: cleaning the bathroom sink
column3: use only the cleaner a grown-up gives you and wear gloves
column4: strong cleaners hurt skin and eyes

column2: you broke a glass on the kitchen floor
column3: stand still, keep others and pets away, put shoes on, and tell a grown-up; pick big pieces with care and sweep the small ones
column4: tiny slivers go far and cut bare feet

column2: picking up broken glass with bare fingers
column3: use a dustpan and brush, and a damp paper towel for tiny pieces; wrap glass in paper before the bin
column4: fingers get cut and wrapping protects the person emptying the bin

column2: you broke your mum's favourite vase while playing
column3: tell the truth straight away and say sorry
column4: hiding it makes trust worse and someone may cut themselves on the hidden pieces

column2: playing ball indoors
column3: play ball games outside or only with a soft ball where allowed
column4: balls break windows, lamps and ornaments

column2: a cracked or chipped glass or mug
column3: do not use it; show a grown-up
column4: it can break in your hand or leave glass in a drink

column2: a mirror fell and broke
column3: it is not seven years of bad luck, that is a superstition; just clean it up carefully
column4: broken glass is the real danger, not luck

column2: a thermometer breaks
column3: tell a grown-up and do not touch the contents; old glass thermometers may contain mercury
column4: mercury is poisonous and needs special cleaning

column2: scissors for crafts
column3: use child scissors, carry them closed and point down, pass them handle first
column4: open blades can poke eyes and cut

column2: a needle or pin found on the carpet
column3: pick it up carefully and put it in a pincushion or give it to a grown-up
column4: someone stepping on it gets hurt, and toddlers and pets swallow pins

column2: razors in the bathroom
column3: never use or play with grown-ups' razors
column4: the blades are extremely sharp

column2: a craft knife or box cutter for opening a parcel
column3: ask a grown-up to open it
column4: retractable blades slip easily

column2: a staple or drawing pin on the floor
column3: pick it up and put it away
column4: bare feet and paws step on them

column2: a used needle or syringe found in the garden or park
column3: do not touch it; tell a grown-up
column4: it can carry dangerous infections

column2: a baby brother picks up a coin, marble or Lego piece
column3: take it from him gently and keep small things off the floor
column4: babies put everything in their mouths and can choke

column2: checking if a toy is too small for a toddler
column3: anything that fits through a toilet roll tube is a choking risk for under-threes
column4: small parts block a small child's windpipe

column2: a toddler is choking and cannot cough or cry
column3: shout for a grown-up and call the emergency number at once
column4: choking needs fast first aid; every second counts

column2: giving a toddler grapes, nuts or popcorn
column3: grapes should be cut into quarters lengthways and whole nuts and popcorn not given to small children
column4: round firm foods fit exactly in a toddler's airway

column2: a balloon has popped and pieces are on the floor
column3: pick up all the pieces
column4: toddlers suck balloon pieces into their throat and choke

column2: your little sister is playing quietly in another room
column3: go and check what she is doing
column4: quiet toddlers are often getting into something dangerous

column2: looking after a younger sibling for a few minutes
column3: stay with them, keep them away from the kitchen, stairs and water, and call a grown-up if worried
column4: small children cannot judge danger

column2: a baby brother pulls the tablecloth
column3: keep hot drinks and heavy things away from the edge and from tablecloths a baby can reach
column4: he can pull hot tea or heavy pots onto himself

column2: your sibling takes your toys
column3: use words, ask a grown-up to help, and take turns
column4: hitting hurts and does not solve the problem

column2: a baby is crying while you are near
column3: do not pick up a baby unless a grown-up says so and shows you how to support the head
column4: a baby's neck is weak and babies are easy to drop

column2: shaking a baby to stop it crying
column3: never shake a baby
column4: shaking causes serious brain damage

column2: nappy cream, wipes and baby lotion within reach
column3: keep them away from the baby's hands
column4: babies eat creams and wipes

column2: a long scarf or string tied around a toddler's toy
column3: keep cords and strings away from small children
column4: they can wrap around the neck

column2: a button battery from a remote or toy
column3: keep button batteries away from little children and throw used ones away safely; if one is swallowed, go to hospital immediately
column4: a swallowed button battery burns through the throat within two hours

column2: small strong magnets from a toy
column3: keep them away from toddlers; if two are swallowed, get medical help at once
column4: magnets inside the body pull together through the gut and tear it

column2: batteries going in the rubbish bin
column3: recycle them at a battery bin in a shop or recycling centre
column4: batteries can leak poison and start fires in bin lorries

column2: a battery is leaking white crusty stuff
column3: do not touch it with bare hands; let a grown-up clean it
column4: the leaking chemical burns skin

column2: putting batteries in a toy
column3: match plus to plus and minus to minus, do not mix old and new
column4: wrong batteries leak or get hot

column2: a phone or tablet battery swells or gets very hot
column3: stop using it, unplug it, put it on a hard surface away from things that burn and tell a grown-up
column4: swollen lithium batteries can catch fire

column2: a magnet near a phone, cards or a laptop
column3: keep strong magnets away from electronics and bank cards
column4: magnets can wipe card strips and damage some devices

column2: playing with a plastic bag over your head
column3: never put a plastic bag over anyone's head, and keep bags away from babies
column4: it sticks to the face and stops breathing

column2: plastic bags stored in a drawer
column3: tie them in a knot and keep them up high
column4: knotted bags cannot be pulled over a head easily

column2: a thin dry-cleaning bag on the bed
column3: throw it away
column4: thin film clings to a baby's face

column2: reusing shopping bags
column3: keep a bag for life in the car or in your schoolbag
column4: it saves plastic and money; many places charge for bags

column2: finding pills that look like sweets
column3: never eat any medicine unless a grown-up who looks after you gives it
column4: medicines can be very dangerous in the wrong dose

column2: someone says medicine is candy to get a toddler to take it
column3: call medicine medicine, not sweets
column4: children then look for more "candy"

column2: your friend has asthma and you want to try their inhaler
column3: never take someone else's medicine
column4: it was chosen for their body and illness

column2: a little brother has swallowed something from the medicine cabinet
column3: tell a grown-up at once; they call poison help or the emergency number
column4: quick help reduces harm

column2: cleaning products under the sink
column3: keep them in their original bottles, locked or high up
column4: children and pets drink them

column2: mixing bleach with another cleaner to make it stronger
column3: never mix cleaning products
column4: bleach with some cleaners makes poisonous gas

column2: warning symbols on a bottle
column3: learn the warning signs: corrosive, toxic, flammable, harmful
column4: they tell you how a product can hurt you

column2: a drink bottle in the garage has an odd liquid inside
column3: never drink from a bottle you are not sure of
column4: people sometimes keep chemicals in old drink bottles

column2: getting a cleaning spray in your eyes
column3: rinse eyes with clean running water for several minutes and tell a grown-up
column4: water washes the chemical away

column2: vitamins taste like sweets
column3: take only the dose a grown-up gives you
column4: too many vitamins, especially iron, can poison a child

column2: you feel ill and want to take a painkiller on your own
column3: ask a grown-up; children's medicines have special doses
column4: adult medicines can harm children

column2: poisonous houseplants and berries
column3: do not eat leaves or berries from plants unless a grown-up says they are food
column4: many garden and house plants are poisonous

column2: e-cigarette refills in the house
column3: do not touch them; tell a grown-up if left out
column4: liquid nicotine is poisonous even in small amounts

column2: matches or a lighter left on the table
column3: do not touch them; give them to a grown-up
column4: they are tools for grown-ups and fires start fast

column2: a lit candle in your bedroom
column3: never leave a candle alone; keep it away from curtains and blow it out before leaving the room
column4: candles cause many house fires

column2: birthday candles on a cake
column3: blow from a safe distance and keep hair back
column4: hair catches fire easily

column2: your clothes catch fire
column3: stop, drop to the ground, cover your face and roll
column4: running fans the flames; rolling smothers them

column2: the smoke alarm goes off
column3: get out, stay out, call the emergency number from outside
column4: smoke kills faster than flames

column2: a smoke-filled room
column3: get low and crawl under the smoke to the exit
column4: cleaner air is near the floor

column2: a closed door during a fire
column3: feel it with the back of your hand; if it is hot, do not open it, use another way
column4: a hot door means fire on the other side

column2: wanting to fetch your tablet or pet during a fire
column3: leave everything and get out; tell firefighters about pets
column4: people die going back inside

column2: a family fire escape plan
column3: know two ways out of each room and a meeting place outside
column4: everyone gets out quickly and you know who is missing

column2: smoke alarm beeps once in a while
column3: tell a grown-up the battery needs changing
column4: a dead alarm cannot warn you

column2: the emergency number to call
column3: 999 in the UK, 999 or 112 in Ireland, 911 in the USA and Canada, 000 in Australia, 111 in New Zealand
column4: you must know your country's number by heart

column2: calling the emergency number
column3: say which service you need, your address, and what happened, then stay on the line
column4: the operator needs facts to send help

column2: pretending to call the emergency number as a joke
column3: never make prank emergency calls
column4: it can stop someone in real danger getting help

column2: a heater with clothes drying on it
column3: keep clothes, towels and toys at least a metre away from heaters and fires
column4: they can catch fire

column2: an open fire or wood stove in the living room
column3: stay back from the fire guard, never put things in the fire without a grown-up
column4: burns and sparks

column2: a fire extinguisher or fire blanket
column3: know where it is, but leave using it to grown-ups; your job is getting out
column4: children fighting fires get hurt

column2: carbon monoxide alarm beeping
column3: open windows, get everyone out and tell a grown-up
column4: carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas with no smell or colour

column2: fireworks at home on Bonfire Night, the Fourth of July or New Year
column3: watch from a safe distance, never pick up a used firework, hold sparklers with gloves and put them in water after
column4: fireworks and sparklers burn very hot

column2: a lawnmower is running
column3: stay well away and never go near the blades, even when it is off; it is a grown-up's job
column4: mowers throw stones and cut off toes

column2: a rake lying with teeth up on the lawn
column3: lay rakes teeth down or hang them up
column4: stepping on it swings the handle into your face

column2: power tools in the garage
column3: never touch drills, saws or hedge trimmers
column4: they cut and crush in an instant

column2: weedkiller and slug pellets in the shed
column3: keep away and wash hands after gardening
column4: they are poisons for people and pets

column2: paint, petrol or antifreeze in the garage
column3: do not touch; antifreeze tastes sweet but is deadly
column4: chemicals poison and some catch fire

column2: a car in the garage with the engine running
column3: never play in a garage with a running car; tell a grown-up
column4: exhaust fumes contain carbon monoxide

column2: the garage door is closing
column3: never run under or play near a closing garage door
column4: it can crush you

column2: playing in or near a parked car
column3: never play in cars; a hot car can kill
column4: cars heat up fast in the sun and children get trapped

column2: a ladder leaning against the house
column3: do not climb ladders without a grown-up holding them
column4: falls from ladders cause serious injuries

column2: gardening gloves
column3: wear gloves when gardening
column4: thorns, splinters, soil germs and insects

column2: a garden pond or paddling pool
column3: never play near water alone; empty paddling pools after use
column4: young children drown in shallow water

column2: a trampoline in the garden
column3: one person at a time, with a safety net, no flips
column4: crashes cause broken bones

column2: a barbecue
column3: stay away from a lit barbecue and never squirt fuel onto it
column4: barbecues stay hot for hours and fuel flares

column2: stinging nettles in the garden
column3: wear long sleeves and avoid them; a dock leaf or cool water soothes a sting
column4: nettles sting skin

column2: spiders and snakes in the shed in Australia
column3: do not reach into dark corners or shoes; tell a grown-up
column4: redback spiders and some snakes are venomous

column2: your house key
column3: keep it safe and hidden, not on a label with your address
column4: anyone who finds it could get in

column2: locked out of the house
column3: go to a trusted neighbour or call a parent; do not climb in a window
column4: climbing is dangerous and looks like a burglary

column2: showing your key to strangers
column3: keep keys private
column4: people could see you are home alone

column2: a hidden spare key under the doormat
column3: do not tell others where the spare key is hidden
column4: burglars check doormats

column2: locking the door when you get home
column3: lock the door behind you
column4: it keeps you safe inside

column2: the front door is left open
column3: close it and tell a grown-up
column4: pets escape and strangers could walk in

column2: losing the house key
column3: tell a grown-up at once
column4: locks may need changing

column2: being left home alone for a short time
column3: only if a grown-up agrees; know when they will be back and how to contact them
column4: the law and advice differ by place, and you need a plan

column2: the doorbell rings when you are home alone
column3: do not open the door; you need not answer; call a parent if worried
column4: strangers can trick children

column2: a phone call asks if your parents are home
column3: say "they can't come to the phone right now" and take a message
column4: do not tell strangers you are alone

column2: being home alone and getting hungry
column3: eat cold snacks and avoid the hob or oven unless allowed
column4: cooking alone causes fires and burns

column2: being home alone and a friend wants to come over
column3: ask a parent first
column4: grown-ups decide who visits

column2: being home alone and scared by a noise
column3: check from a safe place, call a parent; if there is danger, call the emergency number
column4: houses make noises, but danger needs help

column2: someone online asks where you live
column3: never share your address or that you are home alone
column4: strangers online can be dangerous

column2: an emergency contact list on the fridge
column3: keep parents', a neighbour's and emergency numbers in one place
column4: you can find them fast

column2: knowing your own address and phone number
column3: learn your full address and a parent's phone number by heart
column4: you need them in an emergency

column2: a new family moves in next door
column3: say hello and introduce yourself with a grown-up
column4: good neighbours help each other

column2: your ball goes into the neighbour's garden
column3: knock and ask politely to get it back; do not climb the fence
column4: it is their property and fences can break or hurt you

column2: playing loud music late at night
column3: keep noise down in the evening and early morning
column4: neighbours sleep and need quiet

column2: an elderly neighbour lives alone
column3: offer to help with small jobs, and tell a grown-up if you have not seen them for a while
column4: older people can fall and need help

column2: the neighbour's dog barks at the fence
column3: do not tease it or put hands through the fence
column4: it may bite

column2: a neighbour invites you inside alone
column3: check with your parent first
column4: a grown-up should know where you are

column2: kicking a ball against the neighbour's wall or car
column3: play where it does not damage things
column4: it disturbs and damages

column2: picking flowers from a neighbour's garden
column3: ask first
column4: it is someone else's garden

column2: a delivery driver knocks with a parcel
column3: let a grown-up answer; if alone, do not open the door; they can leave a card
column4: it may not be a real delivery

column2: a parcel left on the doorstep
column3: bring it in quickly if a grown-up says so
column4: parcels get stolen

column2: a parcel arrives for a neighbour
column3: take it only if a parent agrees, and give it back the same day
column4: it shows trust

column2: someone at the door says they are from the gas company
column3: grown-ups ask to see ID and can call the company; children do not let them in
column4: criminals pretend to be workers

column2: a food delivery arrives
column3: let a grown-up open the door, pay and check the order and any allergy notes
column4: the grown-up knows what was ordered and can spot a mistake or a stranger

column2: someone selling things at the door
column3: politely say no and close the door, or get a grown-up
column4: door sellers can be scams

column2: feeling cold in winter
column3: put on a jumper before turning up the heating
column4: it saves energy and money

column2: touching a hot radiator or heater
column3: do not lean on or sit on heaters
column4: they burn skin

column2: a portable heater
column3: keep it away from curtains and bedding, never cover it
column4: it can start a fire

column2: hot weather and the house is too hot
column3: close curtains in the day, open windows at night, drink water
column4: keeps the house cool

column2: leaving the air conditioning on with windows open
column3: close windows when the air conditioning is on
column4: it wastes energy

column2: a hot water bottle
column3: fill it with hot, not boiling, water and use a cover
column4: boiling water can burst it and scald

column2: leaving lights on in an empty room
column3: switch off lights when you leave
column4: it saves electricity and money

column2: leaving the TV on standby
column3: switch off at the wall when not in use
column4: standby uses electricity

column2: long showers
column3: keep showers short
column4: saves water and energy

column2: leaving the fridge door open while deciding what to eat
column3: decide first, then open
column4: the fridge warms up

column2: the cat is sleeping on your bed
column3: let it be or move it gently
column4: cats need rest

column2: a dog is eating
column3: leave it alone while it eats
column4: dogs can bite to guard food

column2: chocolate on the table near the dog
column3: keep chocolate, grapes, raisins and onions away from dogs
column4: they are poisonous to dogs

column2: lilies in a vase
column3: keep lilies away from cats
column4: lilies are deadly to cats

column2: the hamster cage door left open
column3: close it every time
column4: hamsters escape and get lost or hurt

column2: pet bowls on the kitchen floor
column3: watch for toddlers eating pet food
column4: they choke or get ill

column2: a toilet seat left up
column3: put it down and close the lid
column4: it is polite and toddlers can fall in

column2: toothbrush shared with a sibling
column3: use only your own toothbrush
column4: germs spread

column2: hair straighteners left on
column3: switch them off and put them on a heat mat
column4: they burn skin and start fires

column2: the toilet roll has run out
column3: put a new roll on
column4: it is polite for the next person

column2: a bathroom without a window gets steamy
column3: turn on the fan and open the door after
column4: damp grows mould

column2: a nightlight or lamp touching the curtain
column3: keep lamps away from fabric
column4: bulbs get hot

column2: eating in bed
column3: eat at the table
column4: crumbs attract insects and make the bed dirty

column2: a toy box with a heavy lid
column3: use boxes with slow-closing lids or none
column4: lids slam on heads and fingers

column2: staying up late with a screen
column3: put screens away an hour before bed
column4: screens make it harder to fall asleep

column2: a fireplace or candle near Christmas decorations
column3: keep decorations away from heat
column4: they catch fire

column2: Christmas tree lights
column3: switch them off at night and when you go out
column4: old or overheated lights start fires

column2: a dog and a toddler on the sofa
column3: keep an eye on them
column4: pets can snap if pulled

column2: the remote control battery cover is missing
column3: tell a grown-up so it can be taped shut or fixed, and keep the remote away from toddlers
column4: toddlers pull batteries out and swallow them

column2: someone knocks on your bedroom door
column3: say "come in" or "just a moment"
column4: it is polite

column2: entering a sibling's room
column3: knock and wait
column4: everyone needs privacy

column2: wearing shoes indoors
column3: follow the family's rule; in many homes people take shoes off at the door
column4: keeps floors clean

column2: a guest visits your home
column3: greet them, offer a drink, and show them where things are
column4: guests feel welcome

column2: you use the last of the milk
column3: tell someone or write it on the shopping list
column4: others need it too

column2: borrowing something from a family member
column3: ask first and give it back
column4: it shows respect

column2: a parent is on an important phone call
column3: wait quietly unless it is an emergency
column4: interrupting is rude

column2: going to bed without saying goodnight
column3: say goodnight to your family
column4: it shows care

column2: a myth that you should put butter on a burn
column3: cool a burn under cool running water for twenty minutes; no butter, ice or toothpaste
column4: butter traps heat and ice damages skin

column2: a myth that plugs are safe once switched off
column3: unplug before touching inside appliances
column4: switches can fail

column2: a myth that a small amount of bleach is fine to drink
column3: never drink cleaning products
column4: they burn the throat

column2: a myth that you can hide under a bed in a fire
column3: get out of the house
column4: firefighters may not find you, and smoke fills the room

column2: a myth that dropping food is fine if picked up in five seconds
column3: germs stick at once; if in doubt, throw it away
column4: the five-second rule is not true

column2: a myth that all doors stop fire
column3: only closed doors slow fire, and fire doors best
column4: an open door lets smoke through

column2: cutting a finger while cooking
column3: press a clean cloth on it, raise the hand and tell a grown-up
column4: pressure stops bleeding

column2: a burn from a hot pan
column3: cool it under cool running water for twenty minutes, then cover with cling film
column4: cooling stops the burn going deeper

column2: bumping your head on a cupboard
column3: tell a grown-up, put something cold on it
column4: head injuries need watching

column2: a nosebleed
column3: sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for ten minutes
column4: leaning back makes you swallow blood

column2: a splinter in your hand
column3: tell a grown-up who can remove it with clean tweezers
column4: dirty splinters get infected

column2: the first aid kit
column3: know where it is kept
column4: you can find it fast

column2: someone is unconscious and not breathing
column3: call the emergency number and follow the operator
column4: the operator tells you what to do

column2: snow and ice on the front steps
column3: walk carefully and tell a grown-up to grit them
column4: icy steps make people fall

column2: a storm with thunder and lightning
column3: stay inside and away from windows; do not take a bath or shower or use corded phones and plugged-in devices until it passes
column4: lightning can travel through pipes and wiring into the house

column2: hurricane, tornado or bushfire warning
column3: follow the family emergency plan and listen to the radio or official alerts
column4: warnings save lives

column2: a flood warning
column3: move up to higher floors, do not walk in floodwater
column4: floodwater can be fast, dirty and electrified
